1.title: The Soil of 1320
1.text: Imagine this. You open your eyes. Smoke. Straw. Cold. England, thirteen-twenty. Ugh. My back.

lines.text: Imagine this.
You open your eyes. Smoke. Straw. Cold.
England, thirteen-twenty.
Ugh. My back.

2.title: Three Promises
2.text: By tonight, you'll reap another man's harvest, be summoned to his court, and see what happens to a man who said no.

lines.text: By tonight, you'll reap another man's harvest,
be summoned to his court,
and see what happens to a man who said no.

3.title: The Cold Half of the Bed
3.text: The other half of the bed is already cold. Alice? She rose before you. She always does.

lines.text: The other half of the bed is already cold.
Alice?
She rose before you. She always does.

4.title: Born Unfree
4.text: On the lord's rolls, you have a name. Walter atte Brook. And one more word. Nativus. Born unfree. Your land, your labour, even your daughters' marriages answer to one man.

lines.text: On the lord's rolls, you have a name. Walter atte Brook.
And one more word. Nativus.
Born unfree.
Your land, your labour, even your daughters' marriages answer to one man.

5.title: Mud, Oak and Smoke
5.text: Look around. Oak posts. Hazel. Mud. No chimney. Every. Single. Morning. The smoke finds its own way out, through the thatch.

lines.text: Look around. Oak posts. Hazel. Mud.
No chimney.
Every. Single. Morning.
The smoke finds its own way out, through the thatch.

6.title: Alice at the Hearth
6.text: Alice is back from the well. Fire's nearly out. Again. She coaxes last night's embers back to life.

lines.text: Alice is back from the well.
Fire's nearly out. Again.
She coaxes last night's embers back to life.

7.title: Four Children, Two Graves
7.text: Four children survive. Joan, fifteen. Already eyeing a boy. I am not! Hugh, nine. Nine and a half! Little Agnes. And the baby, who coughed half the night. Two more lie in the churchyard.

lines.text: Four children survive.
Joan, fifteen. Already eyeing a boy.
I am not!
Hugh, nine.
Nine and a half!
Little Agnes. And the baby, who coughed half the night.
Two more lie in the churchyard.

8.title: Bread, Ale and a Hood
8.text: Breakfast. Dark bread and weak ale. Like chewing a roof tile. Everyone drinks ale. Even the children. Add hose, shoes and a hood. You're dressed.

lines.text: Breakfast. Dark bread and weak ale.
Like chewing a roof tile.
Everyone drinks ale. Even the children.
Add hose, shoes and a hood. You're dressed.

9.title: The Knock
9.text: A knock. Morning, Walter. Boon day. Today? Today. And Walter, your pig was in the lord's barley again. That pig hates me. Gilbert is the reeve. A villein like you, driving his own neighbours.

lines.text: A knock.
Morning, Walter. Boon day.
Today?
Today. And Walter, your pig was in the lord's barley again.
That pig hates me.
Gilbert is the reeve. A villein like you, driving his own neighbours.

10.title: The Village Wakes
10.text: Outside, the village is waking up. One muddy street. Every family has a croft, a pig, and one grudge. Morning, Walter! Morning.

lines.text: Outside, the village is waking up.
One muddy street. Every family has a croft, a pig, and one grudge.
Morning, Walter!
Morning.

11.title: No Clocks
11.text: Nobody here owns a clock. So what time is it? Roughly, morning. Your day is measured by the sun, and the church bell.

lines.text: Nobody here owns a clock.
So what time is it?
Roughly, morning.
Your day is measured by the sun, and the church bell.

12.title: The Lord's Mill
12.text: Your grain must be ground at the lord's mill. One scoop for you, and one for me. That was two for you. The miller takes his toll. And probably a little more.

lines.text: Your grain must be ground at the lord's mill.
One scoop for you, and one for me.
That was two for you.
The miller takes his toll. And probably a little more.

13.title: The Quern Under the Straw
13.text: So you keep a hand-quern hidden under the straw. What quern? Grinding at home is forbidden. At St Albans, an abbot will pave his parlour with confiscated querns. And in 1381, rebels will rip them up.

lines.text: So you keep a hand-quern hidden under the straw.
What quern?
Grinding at home is forbidden. At St Albans, an abbot will pave his parlour with confiscated querns.
And in 1381, rebels will rip them up.

14.title: The Lord's Pigeons
14.text: Those are the lord's pigeons. Only the lord may keep doves. Shoo! Get off! I wouldn't, Walter. They eat your seed corn. You may not touch them.

lines.text: Those are the lord's pigeons. Only the lord may keep doves.
Shoo! Get off!
I wouldn't, Walter.
They eat your seed corn. You may not touch them.

15.title: Ten Men, One Rope
15.text: Every man over twelve is in a tithing. Ten neighbours, answerable for each other. If one of them runs, the others pay.

lines.text: Every man over twelve is in a tithing. Ten neighbours, answerable for each other.
If one of them runs,
the others pay.

16.title: The Lord You Never See
16.text: Sir Roger owns this manor. You may never speak a word to him. Never even seen him. But you will feel him every hour of your life.

lines.text: Sir Roger owns this manor.
You may never speak a word to him.
Never even seen him.
But you will feel him every hour of your life.

17.title: Joan at the Well
17.text: At the well, Joan and the miller's boy are very much not talking. Hello, Joan. Hello. Very noticeably.

lines.text: At the well, Joan and the miller's boy are very much not talking.
Hello, Joan.
Hello.
Very noticeably.

18.title: The Open Fields
18.text: Then you see it. Your land. Not one farm. About thirty narrow strips, scattered across vast unfenced fields. Which ones are mine again?

lines.text: Then you see it. Your land.
Not one farm. About thirty narrow strips, scattered across vast unfenced fields.
Which ones are mine again?

19.title: Ridge and Furrow
19.text: Year after year, the plough heaps each strip into a ridge. Remember these shapes.

lines.text: Year after year, the plough heaps each strip into a ridge.
Remember these shapes.

20.title: The Hayward's Horn
20.text: To the lord's corn! All of you! Here we go. The hayward is calling the village to work.

lines.text: To the lord's corn! All of you!
Here we go.
The hayward is calling the village to work.

21.title: Boon Day
21.text: Today is a boon day. Everyone but your wife must reap the lord's field first. And our wheat? Our wheat waits.

lines.text: Today is a boon day.
Everyone but your wife must reap the lord's field first.
And our wheat?
Our wheat waits.

22.title: The Rhythm of the Sickle
22.text: Grab a fistful. Cut. Lay it down. Step. Again. And again. My back. Until the sun moves.

lines.text: Grab a fistful. Cut. Lay it down. Step.
Again. And again.
My back.
Until the sun moves.

23.title: Small Hands
23.text: Joan binds the sheaves. Hugh chases crows and hauls water. Go on! Shoo! At nine, he's already a labourer.

lines.text: Joan binds the sheaves. Hugh chases crows and hauls water.
Go on! Shoo!
At nine, he's already a labourer.

24.title: The Tenth Sheaf
24.text: Every tenth sheaf is marked and left standing. That one's not ours. It belongs to the Church.

lines.text: Every tenth sheaf is marked and left standing.
That one's not ours.
It belongs to the Church.

25.title: The Hungry Years
25.text: You've seen this field fail. Five years ago, it rained all summer. Seed rotted. Prices soared. People ate their seed corn, then their horses. Perhaps one in ten died. That winter, you buried a child.

lines.text: You've seen this field fail.
Five years ago, it rained all summer.

Perhaps one in ten died.
That winter, you buried a child.

26.title: The Empty Stall
26.text: And now, a plague on the cattle. Oxen are dying across England. Two beasts short. Two. Your plough team can't pull. And the lord's ploughing comes first.

lines.text: And now, a plague on the cattle. Oxen are dying across England.
Two beasts short. Two.
Your plough team can't pull. And the lord's ploughing comes first.

27.title: The Dry Boon
27.text: At noon, the lord feeds his reapers. Bread. Cheese. Maybe herring. Is there ale? On a wet boon, there's ale. And today? Today is a dry boon.

lines.text: At noon, the lord feeds his reapers. Bread. Cheese. Maybe herring.
Is there ale?
On a wet boon, there's ale.
And today?

28.title: Blood on the Stubble
28.text: Agh! My hand! A sickle slips. Hold still. Hold still. No doctor. Just linen and prayer. The coroners' rolls are full of this.

lines.text: Agh! My hand!
A sickle slips.
Hold still. Hold still.
No doctor. Just linen and prayer. The coroners' rolls are full of this.

29.title: The Cloud
29.text: By mid-afternoon, a dark line of cloud. No. Not today. Your own wheat stands ripe, on the far side of the field.

lines.text: By mid-afternoon, a dark line of cloud.
No. Not today.
Your own wheat stands ripe, on the far side of the field.

30.title: The Ale-Stake
30.text: A bush on a pole means Matilda has brewed. Fresh brewed! Come and get it! Ale sours in days, so women brew constantly. Hm. Thin. That's a fine. Thin?! The ale-tasters fine anything thin, or overpriced.

lines.text: A bush on a pole means Matilda has brewed.
Fresh brewed! Come and get it!
Ale sours in days, so women brew constantly.
Hm. Thin. That's a fine.
Thin?!

31.title: Judgement on the Wall
31.text: In church, the wall shows devils dragging sinners into a monster's mouth. Oh. You can't read. You don't need to.

lines.text: In church, the wall shows devils dragging sinners into a monster's mouth.
Oh.
You can't read. You don't need to.

32.title: "Sir" William
32.text: Ah, Walter. Don't forget the tithe. Your priest takes a tenth of your grain, your lambs, even your eggs. Even the eggs? Even the eggs.

lines.text: Ah, Walter. Don't forget the tithe.
Your priest takes a tenth of your grain, your lambs, even your eggs.
Even the eggs?
Even the eggs.

33.title: The Price of a Wedding
33.text: Father, I want to marry him. First, you must pay the lord merchet: a fine for permission to marry. How much? More than you'd like. Some lords even fined unwed mothers.

lines.text: Father, I want to marry him.
First, you must pay the lord merchet: a fine for permission to marry.
How much?
More than you'd like.
Some lords even fined unwed mothers.

34.title: The Hare
34.text: A hare bolts from the stubble. Dinner! Catch it, and you'll be fined. Not dinner. Game belongs to the lord.

lines.text: A hare bolts from the stubble.
Dinner!
Catch it, and you'll be fined.
Not dinner.

35.title: The King's Reach
35.text: Even the king reaches this far. His tax men value your pots and animals. That sack. For the king's army. Will we be paid? Eventually. His purveyors take grain for his wars, and pay late, or never.

lines.text: Even the king reaches this far.
His tax men value your pots and animals.
That sack. For the king's army.
Will we be paid?
Eventually.

36.title: News from the North
36.text: News! The Scots are burning the north! And the king is feuding with his barons! So, nothing about my pig. It all feels very far away.

lines.text: News! The Scots are burning the north! And the king is feuding with his barons!
So, nothing about my pig.

37.title: The Danger in the Ditch
37.text: The real dangers here are ordinary. Open wells. Ditches. Cooking fires. Carts. Agnes! No! Coroners recorded toddlers drowning while their parents worked the harvest.

lines.text: The real dangers here are ordinary. Open wells. Ditches. Cooking fires. Carts.
Agnes! No!
Coroners recorded toddlers drowning while their parents worked the harvest.

38.title: A Seal of Your Own
38.text: Yet you are not powerless. You own a seal. My own mark. Peasants buy, sell and lease land, and the court records every deal.

lines.text: Yet you are not powerless.
You own a seal.
My own mark.
Peasants buy, sell and lease land, and the court records every deal.

39.title: John Cok's Empty Byre
39.text: On the way home, you pass John Cok's house. His byre is empty. His cow is gone. John? And John won't meet your eye.

lines.text: On the way home, you pass John Cok's house.
His byre is empty. His cow is gone.
John?
And John won't meet your eye.

40.title: The Day John Said No
40.text: Three weeks ago, on a boon day, John reaped his own corn instead. My corn was rotting. What was I to do? A small act of defiance. This is what it cost.

lines.text: Three weeks ago, on a boon day, John reaped his own corn instead.
My corn was rotting. What was I to do?
A small act of defiance.

41.title: Distraint
41.text: The court fined him. He couldn't pay. The cow comes with us. So the lord's men took his cow, until he pays.

lines.text: The court fined him. He couldn't pay.
The cow comes with us.
So the lord's men took his cow, until he pays.

42.title: Tomorrow's Court
42.text: Tomorrow, your turn. Walter atte Brook. His pig, in the lord's barley. Amerced. But I didn't even see it! Your own neighbours sit as jurors. And you can't pay.

lines.text: Tomorrow, your turn.
Walter atte Brook. His pig, in the lord's barley.
Amerced.
But I didn't even see it!

43.title: If You Fall Ill
43.text: If you fall sick, the work is still owed. Send a son. Hire a man. Or pay. I'll go, Father. And when you die, the lord takes your best beast. The priest, your second.

lines.text: If you fall sick, the work is still owed.
Send a son. Hire a man. Or pay.
I'll go, Father.

44.title: If You Run
44.text: You could run. Some do. Just keep walking. But the court names you, and orders your family to bring you back. Survive a year and a day in a chartered town, and you might be free.

lines.text: You could run. Some do.
Just keep walking.

45.title: Those Who Fought Back
45.text: And some villages fought back. Our grandfathers were free men! It's in the Domesday Book! They searched for proof, refused services together, and sued their lords. Back to work. They usually lost. But not always.

lines.text: And some villages fought back.
Our grandfathers were free men! It's in the Domesday Book!

Back to work.
They usually lost.

46.title: Half Still Standing
46.text: Released at last, you run to your own strip. Come on. Come on. You reap until you can't see your hands. Half of it is still standing.

lines.text: Released at last, you run to your own strip.
Come on. Come on.
You reap until you can't see your hands.
Half of it is still standing.

47.title: The Widow Next Door
47.text: Next door, Emma lost her husband last winter. She kept his land. Mistress Emma. Have you thought about remarrying? Every day, sir. Every day you ask. But the steward keeps asking.

lines.text: Next door, Emma lost her husband last winter. She kept his land.
Mistress Emma. Have you thought about remarrying?
Every day, sir. Every day you ask.

48.title: Hot to the Touch
48.text: Walter. She's burning up. Hot to the touch. And no physician comes to a villein's cottage. Alice tries a herb. A charm. A saint's name.

lines.text: Walter. She's burning up.
Hot to the touch. And no physician comes to a villein's cottage.
Alice tries a herb. A charm. A saint's name.

49.title: The Lord's Dung
49.text: Before dark, Hugh pens your sheep on the lord's land. Why there, Father? Because their dung manures his fields. Not ours.

lines.text: Before dark, Hugh pens your sheep on the lord's land.
Why there, Father?
Because their dung manures his fields. Not ours.

50.title: Pottage
50.text: Supper is pottage. Peas, beans, leeks and oats, stewed for hours. Pottage again? Pottage again. Bacon, if you're lucky. No potatoes. No tomatoes. Not for centuries.

lines.text: Supper is pottage. Peas, beans, leeks and oats, stewed for hours.
Pottage again?
Pottage again.
Bacon, if you're lucky.

51.title: Spinning by Firelight
51.text: Alice spins wool by firelight, one eye on the cradle. Her hands haven't stopped since before dawn.

lines.text: Alice spins wool by firelight, one eye on the cradle.
Her hands haven't stopped since before dawn.

52.title: Words You Can't Translate
52.text: Pater Noster, qui es in caelis. You pray in Latin. Words you can't fully translate, for a child you can't heal.

lines.text: Pater Noster, qui es in caelis.
You pray in Latin.

53.title: Rain on the Thatch
53.text: Then, rain on the thatch. No. No, no, no. Your wheat is still in the field. Nothing to do but wait for dawn.

lines.text: Then, rain on the thatch.
No. No, no, no.
Your wheat is still in the field. Nothing to do but wait for dawn.

54.title: The Fever Breaks
54.text: Alice banks the fire under ash. Walter. She's cooler. The fever has broken. For tonight.

lines.text: Alice banks the fire under ash.
Walter. She's cooler.
The fever has broken.
For tonight.

55.title: Twenty-Eight Years
55.text: Twenty-eight years from tonight, a plague will kill perhaps half of England. Labour will become precious. And men like you will start to say no. We are not your beasts! Serfdom will die slowly. But it will die.

lines.text: Twenty-eight years from tonight, a plague will kill perhaps half of England.
Labour will become precious. And men like you will start to say no.
We are not your beasts!

56.title: The Furrow Remembers
56.text: You'll leave no portrait. No letter. Maybe one line in a court roll. But walk across an English field today, and look closely. The ridges and furrows you ploughed are still there. So, could you have survived one day as Walter? Tell us in the comments.
